# Diagnosing Turn Signal Intermittency on a 2009 Chevy Malibu

When an automotive diagnostic scan tool is plugged into the OBD-II port under the steering column, it establishes a physical and electrical connection to the vehicle's data bus. While this process is standard for retrieving trouble codes or clearing limp modes, the physical proximity of the connector can sometimes introduce unintended variables. In your specific case involving the 2009 Chevy Malibu LT, the symptom you are describingâwhere the left turn signal requires continuous pressure to activate and the right turn signal fails to cycle automatically after being manually resetâis indicative of a mechanical or electrical latch failure rather than a software logic error.

The flasher module in GM vehicles from this era is a robust electromechanical relay located near the brake pedal assembly or under the dash, depending on the specific trim level. It relies on a physical plunger mechanism to engage and disengage circuits. If you had to hold the lever down for the left signal, the internal switch likely remains engaged because the return spring has lost tension or the mechanical linkage is misaligned. Conversely, if the right signal does not cycle off after manual intervention, the relay may be stuck in a closed position, preventing the circuit from opening to trigger the next flash interval.

It is highly probable that the diagnostic technician did not inadvertently "bump" a wire loose in a way that would cause this specific asymmetry. A simple disconnect usually results in total failure for both sides or affects only one side consistently, but it rarely creates a condition where one side requires constant input and the other refuses to reset without physical manipulation of the lever. This behavior suggests the plunger inside the flasher unit is seated incorrectly or that the contacts are fouled, causing them to stick.

To verify this hypothesis, you should locate the flasher relay box. On many 2009 Malibus, it is mounted on the underside of the driver's side dashboard. Remove the cover and inspect the relay. If your vehicle uses a standard thermal flasher unit (the black cylindrical component with a metal top), try swapping it with a known good unit from another vehicle or borrow one temporarily. If you swap to an electronic flasher module, note that this change alters the behavior of the hazard lights; thermal units often allow hazards to run continuously at high speeds, whereas electronic modules may limit them.

Another potential culprit lies in the turn signal stalk itself. The mechanism inside the steering column handle contains a detent spring and a micro-switch. If the diagnostic tool's connector was plugged directly into the Data Link Connector (DLC) while the ignition was on, or if the technician leaned on the column cover during installation, they could have shifted the internal alignment of the stalk assembly. This would explain why the lever feels different than usual or requires extra force to engage a specific position.

You can test the stalk independently by removing it from the steering column. This involves releasing the two retaining screws at the base of the stalk and pulling the assembly upward carefully. Once removed, manually actuate the switch for both left and right positions while observing the behavior with the headlight switch in "on" mode (not parking lights). If the circuit completes without holding the lever or cycling automatically when disconnected from the column, the issue is definitively within the flasher relay or the wiring harness between the relay and the bulbs.

If the stalk tests normal when isolated, the problem lies downstream. You can perform a continuity check on the bulb sockets to ensure you haven't burnt out a filament in a way that creates a high-resistance path, though this usually results in dim lights rather than cycling failures. The most cost-effective repair is replacing the flasher relay first, as it is inexpensive and fits within the dashboard without requiring disassembly of the steering column.

If replacing the relay does not resolve the issue, inspect the wiring harness for chafing near the firewall or where the harness enters the cabin. Sometimes, a connector can become partially oxidized or loose after vibration over years of driving, but the asymmetry of your symptoms points more strongly toward a mechanical sticking point in the flasher unit itself. Addressing this now prevents potential electrical shorts that could occur if the contacts weld together due to excessive arcing.
